Oath
OHTH
noun
A solemn calling of God to witness the truth of what one affirms or promises; from the Old English āth.

See also: Oath

📖 Biblical Definition

An oath is a solemn calling of God to witness the truth of what one affirms or the sincerity of what one promises, invoking Him as the judge of one’s words. The dictionary follows the Reformed and confessional understanding, which distinguishes the lawful oath from vain and profane swearing. A lawful oath is a part of religious worship, in which the one swearing solemnly appeals to God to witness the truth and to judge him according to the truth or falsehood of what he swears; God Himself commanded, thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and shalt swear by His name, and an oath for confirmation is to men an end of all strife. God Himself confirmed His promise to Abraham with an oath. But the Lord Jesus, when He said, Swear not at all, and James, when he said, swear not, neither by heaven nor by the earth, but let your yea be yea, forbade the rash, casual, and profane swearing by which men in that day laced their common speech with light oaths—not the solemn judicial oath rightly taken before God or magistrate. The dictionary reads the oath as a lawful and weighty act of worship when made of things true and right, in the name of God alone, with reverence; and it condemns the vain swearing—the careless oath, the profane use of God’s name, the false oath—that takes the holy name in vain, which the LORD will not hold guiltless.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A solemn calling of God to witness the truth of one’s word; lawful and an act of worship when rightly made, but vain and profane swearing is forbidden and takes God’s name in vain.

OATH, a solemn calling of God to witness the truth of one’s word.

A lawful oath is a part of religious worship, appealing to God as judge.

Thou shalt fear the LORD and swear by His name (Deu 6:13).

An oath for confirmation is an end of all strife (Heb 6:16).

Christ forbade rash, profane swearing, not the lawful judicial oath.

📖 Key Scripture

Deu 6:13 — "Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God, and serve him, and shalt swear by his name."

Heb 6:16 — "For men verily swear by the greater: and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife."

Mat 5:34 — "But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne:"

Jas 5:12 — "But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Some misread “swear not at all” to forbid every oath, including lawful ones; the confessional reading distinguishes the lawful judicial oath, an act of worship, from the vain and profane swearing Christ condemned.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the right reading of the Lord’s “swear not at all.” Some (the Anabaptists and others) take it to forbid every oath whatsoever, even the lawful oath before a magistrate; but this sets the Lord against the law that commanded swearing by God’s name, against His own confirming of His promise to Abraham by an oath, and against the apostle Paul, who himself called God to witness. The confessional reading, which the dictionary follows, understands the Lord and James to forbid the rash, casual, and profane swearing that filled common speech—the light oaths by heaven and earth, the careless invoking of the holy name—not the solemn judicial oath rightly taken.

The principle to recover is the lawful oath as an act of worship and the gravity of God’s name. A lawful oath, made of things true and just, in the name of God alone, with reverence and in conscience of duty, is good and an end of strife. But the third commandment stands: the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh His name in vain. The careless oath, the profane curse, the false swearing that calls God to witness a lie—these are grave sins against the holy name. The believer’s speech is to be so truthful that his yea is yea and his nay nay, and his rare lawful oath taken with the fear of God.
